newsitem.title: USA: US stocks up, Wall Street in election comfort zone.
newsitem.headline: US stocks up, Wall Street in election comfort zone.

text.p: U.S. stocks were broadly higher at Tuesday's midsession as investors cheered the likelihood today's elections would produce a politically divided U.S. Federal government.

Wall Street had long accepted the likelihood of President Bill Clinton's re-election but worries that he would enter his second term with a Democratic Congress had weighed on markets, which feared a loosening of the federal pocketbook, resulting in deeper deficits and higher interest rates.

The Dow industrials gained 50 points to 6092, triggering NYSE index-arbitrage trading curbs at 1150 EST/1650 GMT. The Nasdaq composite rose 11 points to 1231 and the S&P 500 index surged more than one percent, climbing eight points to 714.

"The fear we would be taking a different course away from lower deficits, lower inflation and subdued economic growth is flying out the window," said Richard Cripps, vice president and chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
While Wall Street favors the deregulatory, low-tax mindframe Republicans tend to bring to government, it enjoys the prospect of political gridlock even more.

The reason is based on the belief that Democrats unchecked would run deep spending-driven deficits while Republicans unchecked would run equally deep deficits by failing to find spending cuts to pair off against their tax cuts.
Instead, the odds favor a government that closely resembles the one now expiring, sustaining a political picture that so far has proven profitable for investors.
"It looks like Republicans will win Congress and that will keep the status quo, an environment Wall Street can live with," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.

Clear evidence of Wall Street's confidence came from the bond market, its purest barometer of inflation and interest rate expectations. At midday the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury stood more than a full point higher, pushing the yield down to 6.58 percent, the lowest since March 26.
Also helping the market was a version of the so-called "January effect," a phenomenon that sends stocks higher in the first days of the year as year-end tax-loss selling abates.
Analysts noted that many mutual funds engage in similar trading patters at the end of October when their fiscal years conclude, producing a similar pattern in early November.
"We have a fairly narrow market (advancing) and that reflects the influence of mutual funds which are still in the first five trading days of their fiscal year," said Cripps.

Breadth remained mixed, with advancing issues outnumbering decliners by a roughly seven to four on the NYSE but running about even on Nasdaq. The less than stellar figures left analysts unconvinced the two-day rally ahead of the election results would necessarily continue after the vote.
"Markets do tend to dip after a presidential election," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
"This is not the time to throw caution to the wind," he added.
Politics from outside the U.S. also played a major part in the activity in at least one individual issue.

The Templeton Russia Fund climbed 1-1/4 to 21-3/4 after doctors involved in Russian President Boris Yeltsin's bypass operation declared the procedure a complete success and said Yeltsin would be able to resume normal work.
